guides.summary: Every foreign visitor must be registered at their place of stay within three days of arrival. Hotels do it automatically; in a private home the host registers…

guides.name: Border and customs: what you can bring in and take out
guides.summary: Cash above the equivalent of 100 million soums must be declared. The essentials on medicines, drones, antiques and mobile phones.

guides.name: Money: soums, cards, ATMs and exchange
guides.summary: The currency is the soum. Visa and Mastercard work in the big cities, but bazaars, taxis and the provinces still run on cash. Change money only at banks and…

guides.name: SIM cards, coverage and IMEI registration
guides.summary: Local SIM cards are sold on presentation of a passport. If your phone runs on a local SIM for more than 30 days, its IMEI must be registered with UZIMEI; on…

guides.name: Internet and useful apps
guides.summary: Taxis, maps, train tickets, translation and government services: the apps worth installing before a trip around Uzbekistan.

guides.name: Getting around: planes, trains, buses and taxis
guides.summary: The high-speed Afrosiyob, overnight sleepers, domestic flights, shared taxis and the Tashkent metro — which option suits which distance.

guides.name: Getting from Tashkent to the regions
guides.summary: Samarkand and Bukhara by Afrosiyob, Khiva and Nukus by plane or night train, the Fergana Valley via the Kamchik Pass — a quick cheat sheet for the main routes.

guides.name: Safety and emergency numbers
guides.summary: The single emergency number is 112, operating nationwide since 2025. Uzbekistan is a calm country to travel in; the main risks are traffic, summer heat and…

guides.name: Tourist police and getting help
guides.summary: Interior Ministry units dedicated to tourist safety work in the main tourist cities. What to do if you lose your passport or run into trouble.

guides.name: When to go: seasons and weather by region
guides.summary: The best months are April–May and September–October. Summer is for mountains and fruit, winter for skiing and empty museums. Quick tips region by region.

guides.name: Dress and etiquette: mosques, hospitality and bazaars
guides.summary: Cover shoulders and knees at religious sites, and women should bring a headscarf. Respect for bread, tea and elders is the backbone of local manners.

guides.name: Health: pharmacies, water and medical care
guides.summary: Don't drink tap water unboiled, guard against sun and heat, and don't skip travel insurance. Pharmacies are everywhere; for an ambulance call 103 or 112.

guides.name: Tipping and prices: what to expect
guides.summary: Restaurants often add a service charge, so an extra tip is optional. Tashkent is pricier than the provinces, and haggling is normal in bazaars.

guides.name: Language and useful phrases
guides.summary: Uzbek is the state language, Russian is widely spoken in cities, and younger people increasingly speak English. The Uzbek phrases you'll use most.
